title: Many Waters
subtitle: The Song of Songs in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
The Song of Songs is a love song, and for more than fifteen centuries Christians have also read it as a song of the soul's love for God. The desert fathers read it slowly in their cells. Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Bernard of Clairvaux, Teresa of Á vila, and John of the Cross heard in it the whole journey of prayer: seeking by night, the dark seasons when God seems gone, the wound of love, and a desire for God that never comes to an end.

This book walks through the Song in thirty-two short poems, in four parts, reading it the way those contemplatives did. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it, standing in a long tradition. Open the Song of Songs alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: the kiss
paintings.epigraph: “your love is better than wine.”
paintings.poem:
the old monks said
this is the holiest song,
too strong for beginners.

they read it slowly,
in their cells,
by one small lamp:

let him kiss me—

not a teaching about God.
God himself,
near enough
to touch the soul.

your love
is better than wine.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the kiss” (Song of Songs 1:1–4)—where the poem notes, “your love is better than wine”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the sunburned soul
paintings.epigraph: “I am dark, but lovely”
paintings.poem:
I am dark,
the soul says.
scorched by the sun.
I tended everyone's vineyard
but my own.

and still—
lovely.

the desert fathers knew it:
first you see how dark you are.
then you hear
that you are loved
anyway.

humility
is the door
to the bridal chamber.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the sunburned soul” (Song of Songs 1:5–6)—where the poem notes, “is the door to the bridal chamber”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: where you rest at noon
paintings.epigraph: “T ell me, you whom my soul loves, where you graze your flock”
paintings.poem:
tell me
where you rest at noon—

in the heat of the day,
when the busy hours
burn everything dry.

I don't want to wander
among a hundred voices
looking for you.

follow the tracks,
he says.
the ones before you
walked this way.

the saints
leave footprints.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (Song of Songs 1:7–8)?

paintings.title: the oasis
paintings.epigraph: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms from the vineyards of En Gedi.”
paintings.poem:
En Gedi:
a spring in the wilderness,
green where nothing should be green.

the hermits went into the desert
not because they hated the world,
but to find
this.

a cluster of blossoms
in the dry places.

the Beloved
is sweetest
where there's nothing else.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the oasis” (Song of Songs 1:14–17)—where the poem notes, “is sweetest where there's nothing else”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the banner
paintings.epigraph: “He brought me to the banquet hall. His banner over me is love.”
paintings.poem:
he brings the soul
into the house of wine.

and over her
not the list of her sins,
not the record of her fasting,
not her failures in prayer—

one word
like a banner:

love.

everything else
the soul has carried in
she can set down
at the door.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the banner” (Song of Songs 2:4)—where the poem notes, “she can set down at the door”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: do not rush the soul
paintings.epigraph: “that you not stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires.”
paintings.poem:
don't stir up love
before it's ready.

the old abbas warned
the eager young monks:
you can't force
the soul's awakening.

sit in your cell.
say your prayers.
wait.

love
wakes
when he wakes it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Song of Songs 2:7 (“wakes when he wakes it”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: the winter is past
paintings.epigraph: “For behold, the winter is past. The rain is over and gone.”
paintings.poem:
rise up, my love.
come away.

after the long winter of the soul—
the dry prayers,
the cold years
when God seemed silent—

a voice at the window:

the winter is past.
the flowers are here.
come.

the mystics called it
the springtime of the soul.
it comes
when he calls it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the winter is past” (Song of Songs 2:10–13)—where the poem notes, “it comes when he calls it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the little foxes
paintings.epigraph: “Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards”
paintings.poem:
the desert fathers watched
the little thoughts—

a flash of pride,
a small resentment,
an idle word,
a wandering eye during prayer.

catch them early,
they said,
while they're small.

watchfulness
guards the vineyard
while it blooms.

and at the end of the vigil:
my Beloved is mine,
and I am his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the little foxes” (Song of Songs 2:15–16)—where the poem notes, “my Beloved is mine, and I am his”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: by night
paintings.epigraph: “I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him.”
paintings.poem:
by night on my bed
I sought him,
and did not find him.

the mystics knew this night:
when prayer is dry,
when every feeling of God
is gone.

so the soul gets up
and keeps seeking—
not because she feels him,
but because she loves him.

and just past the watchmen,
there he is.

the dark night
was the way.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “by night” (Song of Songs 3:1–4)—where the poem notes, “the dark night was the way”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the procession
paintings.epigraph: “in the day of his weddings, in the day of the gladness of his heart.”
paintings.poem:
who is this
coming up from the wilderness
like a column of smoke,
perfumed with prayers?

the soul
coming out of the desert,
rising like incense.

and waiting for her,
the King,
on the day
of the gladness of his heart.

her coming
is his joy.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Song of Songs 3:6–11 (“her coming is his joy”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: how he sees her
paintings.epigraph: “You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you.”
paintings.poem:
the soul sees
every stain.

the Beloved looks
and says:
you are all beautiful.
there is no flaw in you.

not because she's earned it.
because he's washed her.

the saints spent years
learning to believe
that one sentence.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “how he sees her” (Song of Songs 4:1–7)—where the poem notes, “learning to believe that one sentence”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: come down from the heights
paintings.epigraph: “Come with me from Lebanon, my bride”
paintings.poem:
come with me
from the lions' dens,
from the leopards' mountains,

from the high, proud places
where the soul
tries to be strong alone.

the way up to God,
the fathers said,
is down:

humility,
the low valley
where the garden grows.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come down from the heights” (Song of Songs 4:8)—where the poem notes, “the low valley where the garden grows”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the wound
paintings.epigraph: “You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride.”
paintings.poem:
one glance,
and he is wounded.

the mystics dared to say it:
God
is wounded with love
for the soul.

and the soul
is wounded back—

a sweet wound,
a longing
nothing in the world
can heal
but him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the wound” (Song of Songs 4:9–10)—where the poem notes, “can heal but him”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the enclosed garden
paintings.epigraph: “My sister, my bride, is a locked up garden; a locked up spring, a sealed fountain.”
paintings.poem:
a garden locked.
a fountain sealed.

the monks called their cells
this garden:

a closed door,
a small room,
a heart
kept for one.

sit in your cell,
an old abba said,
and the cell
will teach you everything.

the enclosure
isn't a prison.
it's where the spring
runs clear.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the enclosed garden” (Song of Songs 4:12)—where the poem notes, “it's where the spring runs clear”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the garden of virtues
paintings.epigraph: “a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing streams from Lebanon.”
paintings.poem:
pomegranates.
nard and saffron.
cinnamon and myrrh.

the old writers read them
as the virtues:
patience, meekness,
chastity, charity,
growing slowly
in the soul's garden.

and in the middle,
feeding every root,
a well of living water—

not the soul's own strength.
his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the garden of virtues” (Song of Songs 4:13–15)—where the poem notes, “not the soul's own strength. his”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: both winds
paintings.epigraph: “Awake, north wind, and come, you south! Blow on my garden, that its spices may flow out.”
paintings.poem:
come, north wind—
the cold one,
the trial,
the dryness.

come, south wind—
the warm one,
consolation,
sweetness in prayer.

the soul needs both.

only when the wind blows
does the fragrance
spill out.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “both winds” (Song of Songs 4:16)—where the poem notes, “does the fragrance spill out”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: I sleep, but my heart wakes
paintings.epigraph: “I was asleep, but my heart was awake.”
paintings.poem:
I sleep,
but my heart is awake.

the contemplatives loved this line:
the body resting,
the heart still watching,
still listening for him.

and when he knocks,
don't wait
to be comfortable.

the soul hesitated,
opened late,
and he had withdrawn.

sometimes he hides
so we'll seek him
with our whole heart.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “I sleep, but my heart wakes” (Song of Songs 5:2–6), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: wounded and still seeking
paintings.epigraph: “If you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am faint with love.”
paintings.poem:
she searched the city
and came back bruised,
her cloak taken.

the seekers of God
know this road:
the long absences,
the misunderstandings,
the cost.

and still, the only message:

if you find him,
tell him
I'm sick with love.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (Song of Songs 5:6–8)?

paintings.title: altogether lovely
paintings.epigraph: “His mouth is sweetness; yes, he is altogether lovely.”
paintings.poem:
describe him, they ask.

and she tries—
gold, cedar, myrrh—

and runs out of words.

the mystics said
every word about God
falls short,
and then say more anyway,
because love
can't stay quiet.

he is altogether lovely.
this is my Beloved,
and this is my friend.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “altogether lovely” (Song of Songs 5:10–16) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: I am his
paintings.epigraph: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.”
paintings.poem:
at first the soul said:
my Beloved is mine.

now she says it the other way:
I am my Beloved's.

the whole spiritual life
is that turn—

from having God
to being had
by God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “I am his” (Song of Songs 6:1–3)—where the poem notes, “to being had by God”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: rising like the dawn
paintings.epigraph: “Who is she who looks out as the morning, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun”
paintings.poem:
first like the dawn,
then like the moon,
then clear as the sun.

the old teachers saw here
the soul's ascent:

a little light,
then borrowed light,
then light
so full of him
it shines.

no one arrives all at once.
it's a sunrise.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Song of Songs 6:10)?

paintings.title: the only one
paintings.epigraph: “My dove, my perfect one, is unique.”
paintings.poem:
sixty queens,
eighty others,
more than anyone can count—

and still he says:
my dove,
my only one.

the mystery of the saints:
he loves each soul
as if there were
no other soul
in the world.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the only one” (Song of Songs 6:8–9)—where the poem notes, “no other soul in the world”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the first green
paintings.epigraph: “I went down into the nut tree grove, to see the green plants of the valley”
paintings.poem:
he goes down to the grove
to see what's growing—

has the vine budded?
are the pomegranates in bloom?

God tends the soul
like a gardener,
watching for the first green
long before we notice it
ourselves.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the first green” (Song of Songs 6:11)—where the poem notes, “long before we notice it ourselves”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: return
paintings.epigraph: “Return, return, Shulammite!”
paintings.poem:
return.
return.
return.
return.

four times,
the call after her.

the desert fathers said:
the whole life of a monk
is this—
turning back to God,
again,
and again,
and again,
every day.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “return” (Song of Songs 6:13)—where the poem notes, “and again, every day”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: his desire
paintings.epigraph: “I am my beloved’s. His desire is toward me.”
paintings.poem:
we think we're the ones
seeking God.

the soul discovers
the older truth:

his desire
was toward me
first.

all our longing
is an answer
to his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “his desire” (Song of Songs 7:10)—where the poem notes, “is an answer to his”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: early to the vineyards
paintings.epigraph: “Come, my beloved! Let’s go out into the field. Let’s lodge in the villages.”
paintings.poem:
come, let's go out—
the fields,
the villages,
early to the vineyards.

the contemplative life
isn't only the cell.

the one who meets him in silence
walks out at dawn
to find him
in the fields,
in the neighbors,
in the work.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “early to the vineyards” (Song of Songs 7:11–12)—where the poem notes, “in the neighbors, in the work”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: new and old
paintings.epigraph: “At our doors are all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, which I have stored up for you”
paintings.poem:
new fruit and old,
stored up for you.

the old:
the prayers of the fathers,
the psalms,
the wisdom of the desert.

the new:
this morning's prayer,
rising for the first time.

the soul brings both
to the Beloved's door.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “new and old” (Song of Songs 7:13)—where the poem notes, “the soul brings both to the Beloved's door”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: leaning on the Beloved
paintings.epigraph: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?”
paintings.poem:
who is this,
coming up from the wilderness,
leaning on her Beloved?

the soul
coming out of the desert
at last—

not proud,
not strong,
not self-made.

leaning.

the whole art of the desert
was learning
how to lean.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “leaning on the Beloved” (Song of Songs 8:5) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: the seal
paintings.epigraph: “Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm”
paintings.poem:
set me as a seal
on your heart.

love is as strong
as death.

its flame
is the very flame
of the Lord—

the only place
his name appears
in all the song.

the mystics called it
the living flame:
God's own fire,
burning in the soul
and not consuming it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the seal” (Song of Songs 8:6)—where the poem notes, “burning in the soul and not consuming it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: many waters
paintings.epigraph: “Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it.”
paintings.poem:
many waters
can't put it out.

not the floods of sorrow.
not the dry years.
not the long nights of doubt.

and it can't be bought.
give everything you own for it,
and you'd still
come away empty-handed.

this love
is only ever
given.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of Song of Songs 8:7?

paintings.title: the one who found peace
paintings.epigraph: “then I was in his eyes like one who found peace.”
paintings.poem:
they worried
over the little sister:
is she a wall?
is she a door?

and the soul answers, grown now:
I kept myself.

and in his eyes
I found peace.

the Hebrew word is shalom:
not only calm,
but wholeness—

what the hermits went looking for
in the desert,
and found
in his eyes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Song of Songs 8:8–10?

paintings.title: come
paintings.epigraph: “Come away, my beloved! Be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices!”
paintings.poem:
the song ends
without an ending:
come quickly,
like a gazelle
on the mountains.

Gregory of Nyssa said
the soul that loves God
never reaches the end of him—

every arrival
is a new beginning,
every finding
a new seeking.

so the song ends
the way the Bible does:
come.

and the soul
keeps running.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come” (Song of Songs 8:13–14)—where the poem notes, “and the soul keeps running”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?
